The relation of the chapter to the older narrative is settled first. Ellicott reads the opening formula as a mere mark of transition rather than a date, since it does not put these events in direct sequence with the last chapter but has been carried over unaltered from the history both books drew on. He finds a second mark of the same hand in the first verse, where Samuel speaks of taking the bridle of the mother city out of Philistine hands and the chronicler writes instead that David took Gath and her daughter towns, which is an interpretation of a curious phrase rather than a different report. Keil and Delitzsch give that very verse as their specimen of the chronicler's habit of paraphrastic explanation, the figure of the bridle standing for the loss of hegemony and the plain words standing for the figure.

The silence about the Moabites is then faced by both. Keil and Delitzsch call the omission surprising, no reason for it being discoverable, and refuse the usual apology, that the chronicler meant to clear David of a charge of barbarity, on the ground that he does not pass over the like treatment of the captives at Rabbah later in the same book. Ellicott rejects the same apology independently and on the same evidence, adding that a writer possessed with the national hatred of the aliens who had oppressed his people was not likely to judge the slaughter of captive Moabites by a modern standard. On the campaign itself he is minutely textual: the name should be Hadadezer, Hadad being a Syrian god worshipped from the Euphrates to Edom and recognisable in Benhadad, and Zobah lay towards Hamath, somewhere near Emesa, a town the Assyrian annals appear to mention. He prefers this book's thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen to the reading in Samuel, since a kingdom in the great plain of Aram would be strong in both, explains houghing as cutting the sinews of the hind legs to disable the animal, and notes that the hundred chariots David kept were a luxury in Israel, the stud being recruited from Egypt only in the next reign and against an express prohibition.

Henry reads the same victories for their lessons. He sets them against the communion with God in word and prayer recorded just before, so that David goes out conquering and to conquer as Jacob lifted up his feet after his vision, and draws five observations from the sequence of conquests. Those long the enemies of the Israel of God are brought down at last, as all opposing rule and power will be put down by the Son of David. Such is the uncertainty of this world that men lose their power at the moment they think to confirm it, Hadadezer being smitten as he went to establish his dominion. A horse is a vain thing for safety, which David both said and seems to have believed, since he houghed the chariot horses rather than trust them. The enemies of the church are often made to ruin themselves by helping one another, the Syrians of Damascus being smitten when they came to the aid of a losing ally. And the wealth of the sinner is sometimes found to have been laid up for the just, since as the tabernacle was built of the spoils of Egypt so the temple was built of the spoils of the nations, which he takes for a happy presage of the interest the Gentiles would have in the gospel church.
9:
The embassy from Hamath is handled first as a question of names. Clarke notes only that the king called Tou here is Toi in the older book. Ellicott explains the variation by the two Hebrew letters that are constantly confused in manuscripts, decides for the form used here, and reports that the versions wander much further, the Syriac turning the man into a king of the Antiochenes and the Arabic into a king of Antioch, apparently by confusion with an Assyrian name; he adds that a scholar of his own day believed he had read the name on the stones from Hamath then newly brought to the British Museum. The envoy's name he treats the same way: the form here looks right, yet the Joram of Samuel may be correct, since an inscription of Sargon calls a Hamathite king by a name compounded with that of the God of Israel, so the God of Israel was evidently not unknown there. He glosses the errand as blessing, that is pronouncing the victor happy, and observes that the clause about the long war with Hadadezer is curtailed in this account.

The dedication and the Edomite campaign raise two textual points and one of command. Ellicott notes that where Samuel says David dedicated the spoil this book says he brought it, the chronicler avoiding a tautology, and that the nations named should include Edom rather than Aram, which all the versions support and which suits a list meant to cover every people David despoiled; the mention of Amalek he refers either to the old raid or, more probably, to a campaign nowhere recorded. On the next verse the two books diverge further, Samuel saying that David made himself a name on his return while this book credits the eighteen thousand to Abishai in the Valley of Salt; from a comparison of the three accounts he infers that Edom invaded Judah while David was occupied in the north, and that a column was detached southward to meet it. Clarke takes up the same difficulty and resolves it by the law of agency, that a victory won by the general David sent is with propriety ascribed to the commander-in-chief who sent him. Ellicott closes the paragraph by noting that Samuel marks the subjugation more fully, and that the six peoples reduced here had all been enemies of David's ill-fated predecessor.

Henry takes the presents and the preservation as the lessons of the passage. It is our interest, he says, to make friends of those who have the presence of God with them, which is what the king of Hamath did when he courted the favour of a conqueror; and since it is vain to contend with the Son of David, the kings and judges of the earth should be thus instructed, though the presents we bring him are not vessels of silver and gold but our hearts and ourselves as living sacrifices. What God blesses us with we must honour him with, which is why the gifts of friends and the spoils of enemies went alike into the store for building the temple, that being most truly our own which has been consecrated to the Lord. He fastens on the repeated clause that the Lord preserved David whithersoever he went, and answers it with the remark that those are always under the eye of God who have God always in their eye; and he reads the record of judgment and justice as showing why the power was given, not that a man may look great with it but that he may do good with it.
14:
The summary of the reign is read for its tenses and its terms. Ellicott takes the verb as describing a permanent state of things rather than a single act, and distinguishes the pair of words that follow, the first naming the quality and the second the conduct which embodies it. Clarke gives the plain equivalents, the man over the host being general-in-chief and the recorder being the king's remembrancer or historiographer royal, while Ellicott takes the second title back to its root, remembrancer, and reports that the Greek and Latin make him the keeper or writer of memoranda where the Syriac and Arabic of the older book make him a leader or director.

The priests in the list are the chapter's hardest textual knot. Clarke states the traditional solution, that Zadok and the other named man were both high priests, one serving at Gibeon and the other at Jerusalem, and notes that the scribe called Shavsha here appears in Samuel as Seraiah. Ellicott corrects the spelling to Ahimelech son of Abiathar, sets out the difficulty, that elsewhere Zadok and Abiathar are the priests of the reign and that Abiathar was himself a son of the Ahimelech whom Saul had killed at Nob, and then declines the obvious remedy. It has been proposed to reverse the names here and in the parallel passage, but he refuses, because an Ahimelech son of Abiathar is named three separate times later in this same book and may have been acting for his father when so brief a list was drawn up; in the absence of further detail, he says, it would be arbitrary to alter the text of four passages at once.

The guard and the last title are explained from custom and from the chronicler's caution. Ellicott identifies the two companies as the royal body-guard, an office for which eastern kings have always employed foreign mercenaries, notes that Josephus calls them exactly that, and argues from the tribal form of both names, and from the company they keep elsewhere with the Philistines, that the guard was recruited from two Philistine tribes. Clarke reports the same tradition in its fuller rabbinic form, that the captain of the guard presided over both the greater and the lesser council and consulted the sacred lots, and that at his word the archers and slingers went out to battle, the sons of David being the highest in authority. On the final phrase Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree independently that it is a paraphrase: the older book calls the king's sons priests, using the one ordinary word for priests which has just been used of Zadok in its proper sense, and this book substitutes the first at the king's hand. Ellicott doubts the common explanation that the word simply means a secular minister, since under the monarchy the priesthood was drawn close to the crown by its judicial duties and a royal sanctuary's chief priest became a great officer of state, a post worth filling with princes of the blood; the chronicler, writing later, has replaced a term that would by then have given offence.
